Jonny Walker This is a press release from Triumph… (July 22, 2026) — Triumph Factory Racing’s Jonny Walker will be joined by Triumph Motorcycles Brand Ambassadors Sam Sunderland and Ivan Cervantes at the 2026 Red Bull Romaniacs. The trio will tackle the iconic hard enduro event aboard near-stock Triumph Tiger 900 Rally Pro motorcycles. Taking place in Sibiu, Romania, from July 28 to August 1, the 23rd edition of the legendary race will once again push riders and machines to their limits across five days of demanding competition. Following the successful introduction of the Adventure categories in 2025, the Tiger 900 Rally Pro returns to the Carpathian Mountains with minimal modifications. All three riders will compete on near-standard motorcycles, with adjusted stock suspension and a select few upgraded parts being the only enhancements made ahead of the event starting. Ivan Cervantes The race begins with the famous city Prologue before four challenging off-road days featuring steep climbs, rocky riverbeds, technical forest singletrack, and mountain traverses. Walker will contest the premier Adventure Ultimate class, while Sunderland and Cervantes will take on the Adventure Core category. As a Red Bull Romaniacs winner on two previous occasions, Jonny Walker returns looking to build on an impressive debut in the Adventure Ultimate class last year. Riding the Tiger 900 Rally Pro, Walker overcame an early setback before claiming three consecutive off-road stage victories to finish second overall, narrowly missing out on the win and proving the capability of Triumph’s adventure platform in one of the world’s toughest races. Now in his second season with Triumph Factory Racing, the British hard enduro specialist heads back to familiar terrain aiming to challenge for the top step of the podium. Sam Sunderland Ivan Cervantes Two-time Dakar Rally winner and two-time FIM World Rally-Raid Champion Sam Sunderland also returns after a hugely successful first appearance at the event in 2025. Racing in the Adventure Lite class, Sunderland dominated the category by winning the Prologue and every off-road day to secure victory by more than four hours. This year, the Triumph Motorcycles Brand Ambassador steps up into the more competitive Adventure Core class, where he’ll face a significantly tougher challenge as he continues to showcase the versatility of the Tiger 900 Rally Pro. Sam Sunderland Jonny Walker Joining Sunderland in Adventure Core is five-time FIM Enduro World Champion Ivan Cervantes. One of the most decorated enduro riders of all time and no stranger to adventure competition aboard Triumph machinery, Cervantes boasts victories at events including 1000 Dunas, Baja Aragón, and the Bassella Race on the Tiger 900 Rally Pro. Returning to Red Bull Romaniacs for the first time in over a decade, the Spaniard brings a wealth of off-road experience and will be aiming to fight for class honours on his first appearance in the Adventure Core category. Red Bull Romaniacs kicks off with the Prologue on Tuesday 28 July, followed by four gruelling off-road days. Jonny Walker Jonny Walker : “I’m really looking forward to getting back to Romaniacs on the Tiger 900 Rally Pro. I had a lot of fun racing the adventure bike there last year and we came incredibly close to taking the win, so the goal is definitely to challenge for the top step again. I haven’t ridden the bike since last year’s event, so we’ll arrive, make the most of our setup, and get straight into racing, but I do have complete confidence in both the bike and the team. It’s a race I know well and really enjoy, with a tough Prologue and four demanding off-road days, and I can’t wait to get back into the mountains.” Sam Sunderland Sam Sunderland: “I’m really excited to be heading back to Red Bull Romaniacs with Triumph. Last year’s event was a great experience and I was genuinely impressed by what the near-standard Tiger 900 Rally Pro could do in such demanding terrain. Stepping up into the Adventure Core class adds another level of difficulty, and I’m looking forward to seeing what we can achieve against even stronger competition.” Ivan Cervantes Ivan Cervantes: “It’s fantastic to be returning to Red Bull Romaniacs after so many years and to be racing in the Adventure Core class with the Tiger 900 Rally Pro. My first experience of Romaniacs was over a decade ago, so I’m excited to come back with much more experience and a bike that I know extremely well. I’ve enjoyed a lot of success with the Tiger 900 Rally Pro at events like 1000 Dunas, Baja Aragón, and the Bassella Race, so I know what it’s capable of. Adventure Core is a very competitive class, but my goal is simply to give my best and fight for the win.” Ian Kimber – Head of Global Racing Programs, Triumph Motorcycles: “We’re really excited to return to Red Bull Romaniacs again this year. With very little preparation last year with the Tiger 900 Rally Pro machines, Jonny and Sam both had great races, and we enjoyed being part of such a world-renowned, and notoriously difficult event. This year we again race with the same bikes, and we know that Ivan and Sam will want to have positive results in the new class, while Jonny will be aiming for a top result in the Adventure Ultimate category. The Adventure classes had so much interest last year and it was great to see, so we’re looking forward to a great race. We’ve done very little to the bikes in terms of modifications, and this is the best test to show their capability. Roll on next week!” READ MORE Motorcycle Racing Hub → READ MORE Hard Enduro → READ MORE Press Releases → Cycle News Magazine Top Stories Turner Announced as Wild-Card Entry Kawasaki To Unveil KX327X at Loretta Lynn’s 2026 Loretta Lynn's Amateur National Results 2026 Mid-Ohio MotoAmerica Results (Updated) 2026 Industry Speedway Results Latest Videos Press Releases view all > USWE Returns as Official Hydration Pack Partner of the Red Bull Tennessee Knockout for 2026 Norton Motorcycles and Foster + Partners Collaborate to Redefine Motorcycle Retail Kawasaki To Unveil KX327X at Loretta Lynn’s Suzuki Extends Fast Friends Rewards Program Regina Catene Calibrate and KTM Form Technical Partnership MotoAmerica is Live at Mid-Ohio NHRA’S 75th Anniversary Celebration Continues at the Cornwell Quality Tools NHRA U.S. Nationals Husqvarna Factory Racing Extends Agreements With Nestaan and Kay de Wolf Video: We Ride FMF's NEW Husqvarna TE 300 Project Bike

Photograph: Ghana Food Movement View image in fullscreen The Ghana Food Movement's cooking masterclasses offer local people the chance to learn more about traditional Ghanaian food. Photograph: Ghana Food Movement Food security Moringa lattes and tigernut kebabs: the Ghanaians ‘taking back the power’ of their food In Ghana, a grassroots movement is championing nutritious, homegrown, climate-resilient produce, rather than western imports Supported by About this content Kaamil Ahmed Wed 26 Aug 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 07.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A fter three years at catering school, Abiro Wisdom was certain of one thing – he did not want to go into catering. At least not the route that he might be expected to take. His course at Accra Technical University had prepared students for working in international hotels, focusing on French, Italian and Mexican cuisine. The nutritious, homegrown food that Wisdom had eaten while growing up in Bolgatanga, northern Ghana , did not feature at all. “I didn’t see myself there,” he says of the big chain hotels. “I felt I wouldn’t be myself working there – I wouldn’t be able to talk about the food from where I come from.” View image in fullscreen Abiro Wisdom found that his catering course in Accra did not feature the nutritious, homegrown food that he had grown up eating. Photograph: Ghana Food Movement Wisdom instead joined the Ghana Food Movement (GFM), which was founded in 2019 – the year he graduated – and quickly became a champion for Indigenous foods. He says: “We’re a community of food lovers, of believers in the potential of Ghanaian food.” Ghana imports at least half of its food and is heavily influenced by foreign cuisine and ingredients, but Wisdom believes northern Ghana, the country’s agricultural heartland with its huge variety of nutritious and climate-resilient crops and vegetables, could be the secret to the country’s broken food system. The GFM was initially a loose network of volunteers interested in food systems – chefs, farmers, entrepreneurs and experts in food security. In the early days they met in cafes and set up dinners in whatever space they could find to deliver three-course meals often made using a single crop. “[Traditionally] we make tigernut milk, but you can make so many different things, for example tigernut burgers and tigernut kebabs,” says Aimee Wallin, the group’s Malian-Swedish co-managing director. “We want people to taste what we are about, not just talk about what we are about.” The group has been registered as a non-profit organisation for the past five years and now has its own kitchen where it brainstorms new recipes, many of them thought up by Wisdom. It runs monthly pop-ups and dine-and-dance nights, as well as panel discussions and recipe testing events for chefs and local businesses. Wisdom says: “We might brainstorm ideas around a single food, such as moringa leaves, to show how it’s possible to sell – and make a profit from – dishes and drinks using Indigenous ingredients.” View image in fullscreen The Ghana Food Movement’s spice making workshop with Indigenous alligator pepper, egusi seeds and ginger shavings among other ingredients. Photograph: Ghana Food Movement The GFM has started working with schools, helping children appreciate local ingredients. Wisdom hopes this multi-pronged approach will help instil more national pride in Ghanaian food. “My goal is that we have a generation of chefs who believe in Ghanaian food and its own identity,” he says. “I’ve come to understand how food contributes to politics, to the economy, how it contributes to self-identity. [Now I can] trace the impact of food on our society, on our land, to the sea, to the farmer, down to how the food gets to the market, then to our plates. As chefs, we have to be able to tell the story of the food.” This month the group won a Champions of Change title in the 50 Best Restaurants Awards in recognition of the transformational work it is doing. View image in fullscreen The Ghana Food Movement’s dine-and-dance night at The Kitchen, which it opened in Accra in 2024. Photograph: Kyei Baidoo/Ghana Food Movement Foreign, colonial influence has played a heavy role on African food systems , when ruling powers dictated land should be used for cash crops for export, such as cocoa or peanuts, at the expense of food for local consumption. At the same time, they put more value on imported ingredients such as rice, disrupting the sustainability of countries’ food systems. The impact has continued to modern times, making African countries heavily reliant on imports and vulnerable to price shocks when wars or other crises disrupt shipping. But, as Wisdom discovered at university, there is also a lingering cultural influence, with western food still taught in culinary institutes and sought after in restaurants. Africa’s small-scale revolution against big agriculture: five farmers talk greener, better food Read more “The narrative has always been that our practices are wrong and the west’s practices are right. It’s just super-stupid. Why would you do that when you can just grow your own food?” says Wallin. “Part of the postcolonial agenda is for us to still have to depend on other countries. If it’s not to buy their products, to buy their vegetables, then at least we need to buy their seeds and their pesticides and their fertilisers,” says Wallin, who points out that many of the local ingredients they champion do not need extra agricultural inputs because they are adapted to the local environment. “The one who feeds us will control us and that’s how it is today. So, if we want to control ourselves, we also need to feed ourselves. It’s power. Taking back the power of our foods and using it to our advantage.” For younger Ghanaians there is a new international pull towards heavily advertised trends and social media fads such as matcha lattes, bubble tea and smash burgers. View image in fullscreen The chefs often highlights one local ingredient in three or four different courses, such as plantain. Photograph: Kyei Baidoo/Ghana Food Movement Wallin says that also offers a culinary opportunity – to earn the interest of young people, by offering alternatives, replacing matcha with moringa lattes or making shawarma out of tigernut instead of meat. Both Wallin and Wisdom believe that their movement has the urgent task of saving Ghana’s food heritage before knowledge is lost. “If we want to talk about what our future food system should look like,” says Wallin, “we need to talk to our grandmas, to our grandpas, to the farmers out in the communities because they sit on that knowledge. If we don’t talk to them now, it’s going to be too late. So it’s really like now or never.” Explore more on these topics Food security Ghana Food Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-launches-o.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ityt Ukraine has increasingly stepped up its attacks on infrastructure within Russia (FILE: 16.08.2026) Image: Stringer/REUTERS Advertisement Hundreds of drones targeted the Moscow region in a sustained overnight assault that killed at least six people, according to the Russian capital's mayor, as Ukraine steps up long-range attacks deep inside Russia. Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 600 drones had flown toward the Moscow region between Saturday evening and 6:30 a.m. local time (0330 UTC) on Sunday, adding that 201 were destroyed over the region. What happened in Moscow drone attack? Russia said five people had been killed in Ukraine's attacks, five in the southwestern city of Rostov and one in the Moscow region. Sobyanin said three people were wounded in the area inside Moscow's MKAD ring road and were receiving medical treatment. Ukraine has intensified long-range strikes inside Russia in recent weeks, targeting military and industrial facilities as well as warehouses far from the front line. Ukraine's Kyiv Independent newspaper reported that Ukrainian forces had targeted a warehouse belonging to Russian online retail giant Wildberries , as well as industrial facilities in several cities across the Moscow region. There was no immediate independent confirmation of the scale of the attack. Where did Russia attack in Ukraine? Russian attacks have killed at least five people and wounded dozens more across Ukraine, according to Ukrainian officials. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a missile strike on his hometown of Kryvyi Rih killed two people and injured 14 others, while another person was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy. How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure," Zelenskyy said. Zelenskyy said the Russian missile attack on Kryvyi Rih caused multiple casualties, with emergency services responding at the scene. The city, a major industrial center in central Ukraine, has repeatedly been targeted during the war. In the southern Zaporizhzhia region, a man and a woman were killed when a Russian strike hit their home, regional military administration head Ivan Fedorov said. Spanish fighter jet shoots down drone over Romania The attack came as NATO countries on Ukraine's borders faced fresh drone incursions of their own. Romania's Defense Ministry said a Spanish F-18 fighter jet shot down a drone early Sunday after it entered Romanian airspace from Moldova near the border with Ukraine. The aircraft was operating on NATO duties and intercepted the drone at 5:01 a.m. local time (0201 UTC). Debris fell in an unpopulated area of Galati county, close to the Ukrainian border. Romanian authorities did not immediately identify the drone's origin or say who launched it. Romania has repeatedly reported drone debris on its territory since 2023 following Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports along the Danube. On Friday, an Italian Eurofighter operating under NATO command also shot down a foreign drone that entered Latvian airspace . Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah Don't let the algorithm hide the news. (OSV News photo/Jakub Wlodek/Agencja Wyborcza.pl via Reuters) Church and Poland mourn after mass shooting in Krakow's historic Main Market Square Katarzyna Szalajko, OSV News World Sunday 8th of November 2026 Listen to this article now Your browser does not support the audio element. (OSV News) -- Six people were killed and over a dozen wounded in Poland Nov. 7 when a gunman opened fire at random passersby in Kraków's Main Market Square, turning one of Europe's best-known pilgrimage and peaceful tourist destinations into a scene of terror. Faced with horror unfolding just meters from his residence, the city's cardinal urged his countrymen to stand together amid "terrible" violence. "We do not want to be, we cannot be, and we are simply unable to be indifferent at a time like this. We want, we need, and we must stand together," Cardinal Grzegorz Rys wrote from the historic Archbishops' Palace of Kraków, located roughly 260 feet from the Main Market Square. In his Nov. 7 statement, Cardinal Rys said that anyone could have been walking through the square when the shooting began, passing "through places where bullets had struck unsuspecting, innocent bystanders." Archbishop Tadeusz Wojda of Gdansk, president of the Polish bishops' conference, also expressed shock at the violence. "I stand in spiritual solidarity with all those who suffered in this exceptionally brutal act and support them with my prayers," he said. -- Scenes unimaginable for a peaceful, tourist city -- Horrific accounts of witnesses of the tragedy started being published soon after the event, in a nation mostly spared of such violent terror events and considered one of the most peaceful places in Europe. Advertisement "He got out of the car and started shooting at people. He was firing at the outdoor cafe tables, where people were sitting and drinking coffee," Dominik Bartelak, of Cafe Una on the Main Market Square, told OSV News. "Bodies were lying near our cafe. A woman was killed near St. Mary's Basilica." He added, "A helicopter landed on the Small Market Square, and someone was being resuscitated right next to us." The shooting started on the corner of the main square where Bartelak's cafe is located. "If someone had been sitting in the chair by our cafe window, they would have been hit. A bullet went through," Bartelak said. When he spoke to OSV News, Bartelak was still inside his cafe, comforting shaken employees and offering hot tea to police officers working at the scene. Reacting to the tragedy, Bishop Artur Wazny of Sosnowiec wrote on X: "I am thinking of those whose lives were taken today with a brutality incomprehensible to the human heart," and the families for whom "the cruelest reality is that the world will keep turning -- only now, it will go on without someone who was irreplaceable." -- Suspect opened fire at random on passersby -- The attack began shortly after 3 p.m., when a man drove into the Main Market Square from the direction of Slawkowska Street and opened fire on people passing by, according to police. The death toll, initially reported as five, rose to six later in the afternoon. Fifteen people were wounded, most of them seriously, including two police officers. Shortly before 10 p.m. local time, Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced that the suspect also killed his parents and sister before he left his family home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski. Katarzyna Cislo, spokeswoman for the Kraków Police, said the suspected gunman was a 25-year-old Polish citizen. "He was using a military-type long gun. A large number of other firearms, as well as ammunition, were recovered from his vehicle," Cislo told Polish media. The attacker was dressed in military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defense Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz strongly denied reports that the gunman had served in the Polish military. "The man was not and is not a soldier in the Polish Armed Forces and has never had anything to do with the military," he wrote on X. Police shot and arrested the suspect. The motive for the attack had not yet been established, although Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said the suspect had been fascinated by far-right ideologies and held "radical views." The attack has already drawn tentative comparisons with Anders Behring Breivik, the Norwegian far-right extremist responsible for the 2011 mass killings of 77 people. -- Special Sunday Mass in St. Mary's Basilica -- Cardinal Rys called for prayers for those killed and injured and asked parish priests to provide support and comfort to the victims' families. He invited residents to a special Sunday Mass at St. Mary's Basilica, overlooking the square where the attack unfolded. "Our faith ensures that we are never -- even in the face of the greatest challenges -- truly helpless," Cardinal Rys wrote. He expressed hope that "the final word does not, and cannot, belong to hatred." U.S. Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose condemned what he described as "a savage and murderous attack" that had shattered the country's peace. "America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Krakow," Rose wrote on X. Mass shootings are extremely rare in Poland, which the U.S. State Department describes as generally safe for visitors. In Warsaw, authorities announced additional security measures, including barriers along streets in the capital's historic Old Town, following the Kraków attack. Kraków is one of the most popular pilgrim destinations in Europe, with dozens of church architectural pearls around its Old Town, as well as places connected to St. John Paul II, who was archbishop of Kraków between 1964 and 1978, when he was elected pope. -- Condolences poured in from across Europe -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was among the many European leaders who condemned the shooting, calling it "a shocking crime." "There can be no justification for this attack, and we trust the perpetrator will face justice," he wrote on X. "People have the right to safety." French President Emmanuel Macron also expressed solidarity with Poland. "Shock and sorrow after the tragic shooting in Krakow," he wrote on X, offering his condolences to the victims and their families. Bishop Wazny concluded his message of condolences: "Lord Jesus, embrace those who are weeping, and teach us to be Your arms for Kraków." - - - Katarzyna Szalajko writes for OSV News from Warsaw, Poland. https://www.kyivpost.com/post/89370.text: North America Latin America Europe Eastern Europe Middle East Africa Asia Business Technology Finance Energy Agriculture Reviews EN UK INTERVIEW Poland Ukraine History ‘This Is Not About Meeting Halfway’ – Poland and Ukraine’s History Dispute In brief: The dispute is not about numbers alone, but about acknowledging the facts and confronting the past. This is an interview with Wojciech Konończuk, director of the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW). By Michał Kujawski by Michał Kujawski | Nov. 8, 2026, 12:04 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Wojciech Konończuk, director of the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW). (Photo courtesy of Wojciech Konończuk) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Below is an interview with Wojciech Konończuk, director of the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW), on Ukraine’s historical disputes with Poland – and how reconciliation might take place. Michał Kujawski: What is the main point of contention in the Polish-Ukrainian dispute over the Volhynia massacres today? Is it the historical findings themselves, the way they are interpreted, or perhaps the emotions involved? JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Wojciech Konończuk: I think it is a bit of everything. Emotions are running high, as has been particularly evident since late May 2026, when President Zelensky named a military unit after UPA heroes. The root cause of the dispute, however, lies in an issue often presented as a debate between historians from the two countries, but that is an oversimplification. It is a dispute between Polish historiography, where there is a consensus, and the dominant strand of Ukrainian historiography over what happened between Poles and Ukrainians during WWII. Advertisement Ukrainian historiography goes hand in hand with the official state narrative, which holds that there was a Polish-Ukrainian war and that both sides committed atrocities. According to this narrative, it was not a planned ethnic cleansing campaign but a fratricidal conflict. This is an attempt to create a false equivalence between the two sides. The Second Polish Republic’s policies towards the Ukrainian minority and Ukrainian citizens were not fair and were often outright discriminatory. There were also reprisals carried out by the Polish Home Army (Armia Krajowa, AK) in Volhynia. Other Topics of Interest New Round of Ukraine Talks Set, European Representatives to Participate No date or venue has been announced for the next round of trilateral talks yet, although Witkoff confirmed it will include European partners. It is true that the Second Polish Republic’s policies towards minorities were as you describe them, but it is worth emphasizing that this is not a subject of controversy in Poland. Poles know about it, we write about it ourselves, and it is covered in school textbooks. There is no dispute about the false and discriminatory policy of interwar Poland towards ethnic minorities, including Ukrainians. Advertisement There were also reprisals against the Ukrainian population during WWII. Were they coordinated, and did the military leadership approve of them? Actions targeting Ukrainian civilians were condemned and, above all, prohibited at the command level of the Home Army. On the territory of present-day Ukraine, the number of Polish victims was much higher. We are talking about 80,000-100,000 Polish victims and 3,000-4,000 Ukrainian victims. “Every victim matters, but this is not simply about numbers.” But if we consider what happened in what is now Poland, the number of Ukrainian victims was around 6,000-8,000, [and] Polish victims 4,000. Does focusing on the number of victims not ultimately lead to a public debate in which the two sides compete over whose suffering was greater? Every victim represents a tragedy, and definitions of ethnic cleansing do not make its classification dependent on the scale of the crime or the absolute number of victims.
